records.d: Pepper's Ghost, demonstrated by John Henry Pepper in 1862, projected ghostly 3D figures onto a Victorian stage with angled glass: the first popular 3D illusion. Audiences gasped at apparitions. The dream of images with depth is 160 years old.
records.h: A large sheet of glass angled across the stage reflected a hidden lit actor, superimposing a translucent figure on the scene. The illusion was optical, not digital. Depth without screens was the goal from the start.
records.mj: Established - documented 1862 Pepper demonstration; theatrical 3D illusion.

records.d: Dennis Gabor invented holography in 1947, recording light's phase as well as intensity so images carried true depth. The word meant 'whole writing.' The physics of real 3D images was born.
records.h: Interference between a reference beam and light scattered from an object recorded a pattern encoding full wavefront information; illumination reconstructed the 3D image. Gabor won the 1971 Nobel Prize. Depth became recordable.
records.mj: Established - documented 1947 Gabor invention; 1971 Nobel Prize.

records.d: In 1962, Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks made the first laser holograms: sharp 3D images viewable in normal light. The laser made holography practical. Real 3D photographs existed.
records.h: Laser coherence enabled off-axis holograms with clear, bright 3D reconstructions. The images showed parallax: moving your head revealed new angles. The hologram became a medium.
records.mj: Established - documented 1962 Leith-Upatnieks laser holograms.

records.d: Ivan Sutherland's Sword of Damocles, built in 1968, was the first head-mounted 3D display: wireframe rooms rendered per eye. The headset was so heavy it hung from the ceiling. Personal 3D displays began as ceiling-mounted experiments.
records.h: Two CRTs rendered stereoscopic wireframes tracked to head position by mechanical sensors. The computer drew the world twice, once per eye. The HMD proved 3D could be worn.
records.mj: Established - documented 1968 Sutherland system; first HMD.
records.t: 1968: the Sword of Damocles - First 3D Headset

records.d: Star Wars in 1977 showed Princess Leia as a flickering hologram: 'Help me, Obi-Wan.' The image set the public's expectation of 3D displays for 50 years. Fiction defined the product before the product existed.
records.h: The film's hologram was a cinematic effect, not a technology, but it gave engineers a target: free-floating 3D video. Every volumetric display since has been measured against Leia. Culture wrote the spec.
records.mj: Established - documented 1977 film; the iconic hologram scene.
records.t: 1977: the Leia Hologram - Fiction Sets the Goal
records.z: timeline|year=1977|span=1|events=Star Wars hologram scene~fiction defines the goal

records.d: Lenticular 3D prints and cards, mass-market in the 1980s, showed depth and motion without glasses: ridged plastic lenses directed different images to each eye. 3D went pocket-sized. The baseball card had depth.
records.h: Lenticular lenses interlaced multiple views so each eye saw a different image, creating parallax depth. No electronics needed. The print proved consumers wanted glasses-free 3D.
records.mj: Established - documented 1980s lenticular prints; glasses-free 3D.

records.d: IMAX 3D in the 1990s brought giant-screen stereoscopic films to museums and malls: depth at architectural scale. The 3D image went huge. Audiences paid premiums for parallax.
records.h: Dual 70mm projection with polarized glasses delivered high-resolution stereo to giant screens. Documentaries led. Scale made 3D an event.
records.mj: Established - documented 1990s IMAX 3D; large-format stereoscopic cinema.

records.d: FogScreen, launched in 2002, projected images onto a thin curtain of fog: walk-through projections you could pass your hand through. The screen became immaterial. 3D's ancestor was a curtain of mist.
records.h: Laminar-flow fog created a projection surface from dry mist, with images appearing to float in air. The screen was literally thin air. The immaterial display was born.
records.mj: Established - documented 2002 FogScreen launch; fog projection display.

records.d: Actuality Systems' Perspecta, shipping around 2005, was the first commercial volumetric display: a rotating screen rendering true 3D images viewable from 360 degrees. Real volumetric display reached the market. The dome showed depth you could walk around.
records.h: A high-speed projector painted slices onto a rotating diffuser screen, building a true 3D image in a glass dome. No glasses, full parallax. Medical and military visualization bought in. The volume was real.
records.mj: Established - documented Actuality Systems Perspecta; first commercial volumetric display.

records.d: In 2010, 3D TV boomed: manufacturers shipped stereoscopic televisions with glasses, and Avatar's success promised a depth revolution. Millions bought in, then stopped wearing the glasses. The boom taught the industry that 3D must be glasses-free.
records.h: Active-shutter and polarized TVs rendered stereo pairs while content struggled to arrive. The glasses were the friction. The market's rejection was the lesson: comfort beats depth.
records.mj: Established - documented 2010 3D TV boom and decline; glasses friction.

records.d: Looking Glass Factory, founded in 2014, built desktop holographic displays showing 3D without headsets: lenticular light fields for creators. The desktop hologram became a product. 3D content gained a native monitor.
records.h: Lenticular arrays over high-resolution panels rendered dozens of views, creating glasses-free 3D for one or more viewers. Creators previewed 3D natively. The monitor learned depth.
records.mj: Emerging - real company and products; desktop holographic displays.

records.d: Microsoft announced HoloLens in January 2015: a self-contained holographic computer overlaying 3D on the real world. Mixed reality went untethered. The 3D image left the screen for the room.
records.h: Waveguide optics projected stereo images while depth sensors mapped the room, anchoring holograms to real surfaces. No PC, no wires. The computer became eyewear.
records.mj: Established - documented January 2015 announcement; self-contained holographic computer.

records.d: In 2015, Japan's Burton Inc. demonstrated laser-induced plasma volumetric displays: 3D images drawn in mid-air with laser pulses. Real images in real air, no screen at all. The Leia hologram got a laboratory proof.
records.h: Femtosecond laser pulses ionized air into glowing plasma dots, scanned fast enough to draw 3D shapes. Touching the image was possible. Mid-air touchable 3D was demonstrated.
records.mj: Established - documented 2015 Burton demonstrations; laser plasma volumetric display.

records.d: By 2017, spinning LED hologram fans were everywhere in retail: floating 3D-looking product images in store windows. The fake hologram went mass-market. Persistence of vision became advertising.
records.h: Rapidly spinning LED bars painted images in the air through persistence of vision, appearing to float. The effect was 2.5D, not true volume, but the price was right. Illusion beat physics on cost.
records.mj: Established - documented retail adoption; spinning LED hologram fans.

records.d: Voxon's VX1, launched in 2018, was a true volumetric display for developers: a high-speed reciprocating screen rendering 3D volumes. The hacker volumetric display. Developers could finally build for real volume.
records.h: A screen swept rapidly through a volume while a projector painted slices, building true 3D images viewable from all sides. The SDK invited experiments. The volume became a platform.
records.mj: Emerging - real shipped product; developer volumetric display.

records.d: Sony's Spatial Reality Display, launched in October 2020, gave creators a glasses-free 3D monitor with eye tracking: the hologram desk display. Professional 3D preview went glasses-free. The workstation gained depth.
records.h: Eye tracking steered a lenticular stereo image to the viewer's eyes in real time, maintaining the 3D effect as they moved. Creators saw models in depth. The monitor watched back.
records.mj: Established - documented October 2020 Sony launch; eye-tracked 3D display.
records.z: timeline|year=2020|span=1|events=Sony Spatial Reality Display launches~eye-tracked glasses-free 3D

records.d: By 2022, volumetric capture stages were recording people as full 3D assets: dozens of cameras building holographic performers. The content pipeline for volumetric displays matured. Holograms gained a supply chain.
records.h: Camera arrays captured performers from all angles, reconstructing textured 3D models per frame. The output fed volumetric and AR displays. Capture became infrastructure.
records.mj: Emerging - real operating stages; volumetric capture pipeline.

records.d: Apple announced Vision Pro in June 2023: spatial computing with micro-OLED 3D at unprecedented fidelity. The trillion-dollar company bet on worn 3D. The headset became Apple's next platform.
records.h: Dual micro-OLED displays with eye and hand tracking rendered spatial apps in the user's environment. The price was premium; the signal was mainstream. Spatial computing got the Apple treatment.
records.mj: Established - documented June 2023 announcement; Apple spatial computer.

records.d: By 2024, research labs were demonstrating computer-generated holography with neural networks: real-time holographic video from learned models. The Gabor dream approached video rates. Computation attacked the hologram problem.
records.h: Neural holography models computed interference patterns in real time for holographic displays, bypassing slow iterative algorithms. The math got fast. True holographic video entered the lab.
records.mj: Emerging - real research; neural real-time holographic video.

records.d: By 2025, consumer light-field monitors were maturing: glasses-free 3D displays for gaming and creation at falling prices. The 3D monitor left the pro studio. Depth became a consumer spec.
records.h: Improved lenticular and light-field panels with eye tracking brought glasses-free 3D to consumer price points. Gamers and creators adopted. The monitor's third dimension went mainstream.
records.mj: Emerging - real maturing products; consumer light-field displays.
